target.definition: Total U.S. utility-scale net electricity generation (all sectors, all energy sources, excluding small-scale solar) during July 2026, as first reported in EIA's Electric Power Monthly Table 1.1.

inputs.name: us_annual_generation
inputs.description: Total U.S. utility-scale net generation in a recent full year (2025)

provenance.rationale: Recent US utility-scale generation runs near 4.2-4.3 million GWh/year, growing ~2%/yr

inputs.name: july_share_of_annual
inputs.description: Fraction of annual generation occurring in July (summer peak month)

provenance.rationale: July is typically the highest-demand month, ~9% of annual output

inputs.name: us_population
inputs.description: U.S. resident population in 2026

inputs.name: per_capita_monthly_generation
inputs.description: Utility-scale generation per person per month in July

inputs.name: peak_summer_demand
inputs.description: U.S. peak summer electricity demand (all sectors)

provenance.rationale: US summer peak demand is roughly 700-750 GW

inputs.name: july_hours
inputs.description: Hours in July

inputs.name: load_factor
inputs.description: Ratio of average to peak load in July

inputs.name: us_gdp
inputs.description: U.S. nominal GDP in 2026

inputs.name: electricity_intensity
inputs.description: Electricity generation per dollar of GDP

provenance.rationale: US uses ~0.13-0.14 kWh per nominal GDP dollar

inputs.name: july_gdp_share
inputs.description: Fraction of annual GDP activity occurring in July

paths.description: Annual utility-scale generation allocated to July by its seasonal share
Peak demand times July hours times load factor

problems: path p2: dimension mismatch: the formula gives mass * length**2 per time**3 (kg*m**2*s**-3), but the target needs mass * length**2 per time**2 (kg*m**2*s**-2). The formula has one 'per time' more than the target; inputs with a time unit in this path: per_capita_monthly_generation ('MWh/person/month'). If the target is a total over a period, multiply by an input whose unit is a length of time: the period itself (for example days_in_period with unit 'day'), or period_length = 1 with unit 'year' when a share of the year then picks the part you need. A share, or a ratio such as 'days/year', has no time unit and does not cancel it.
